newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's UDF names cabinet, pledges reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's UDF names cabinet, pledges reforms.

text.p: Bulgaria's prime minister designate Ivan Kostov on Monday presented his proposed government lineup to President Petar Stoyanov and promised to implement vital economic reforms begun by an interim cabinet.

The list, to be presented to parliament on Wednesday, includes five ministers from the interim cabinet which has governed since mass protests forced out the former Socialist administration in February.

"Bulgaria is coming out of a unique political crisis, a crisis which led to February 4 when a national consensus was reached on the country's main priorities. Now we have a golden opportunity to develop these national priorities into a national programme," Kostov told reporters.

The new government has promised to implement reforms prescribed by the International Monetary Fund, fight organised crime, return land to its pre-communist owners, and bring Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.
Kostov's nominee for finance minister is Muravei Radev, a leading member of his Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) and deputy chairman of the last parliament's economic commission.
Interim deputy premier Alexander Bozhkov retains the industry portfolio, with the task of restructuring the unwieldy state sector and closing or privatising loss-making firms.
UDF deputy chairwoman Nadezhda Mihailova becomes foreign minister, and interim interior minister Bogomil Bonev will continue his high-profile campaign against organised crime.
A new state administration ministry will oversee measures to reduce bureaucracy and improve the flow of information.
One of the new government's first tasks will be to introduce a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime prescribed by the IMF to restore confidence in the lev.

"By July 30, we hope to adopt the most important laws for a currency board and economic stabilisation in order to meet the requirements of the international financial institutions and to be able to receive the second tranche from the IMF," Kostov said.
In April, the IMF approved a stand-by credit worth $510 million. The first tranche of $31.7 million was released immediately, with a $147 million emergency credit to buy grain.

The Financial Stabilisation Council advising the interim cabinet proposed pegging the lev to the German mark in the currency board, though the final decision must be made by Kostov's government and the new parliament, in which the UDF has a big majority.

"The mark will ease Bulgaria's integration in the European monetary system in the future, despite the current prevalence of dollar transactions," said Galina Dimitrova, economist at the Bulgarian Investment Bank.

The deputies, of whom 167 are new to parliament, must also approve a 1997 budget. The interim cabinet has brought inflation back under control, and the lev has recovered from historic lows reached at the height of the crisis in February.

The central bank intervened to support the lev on the interbank market on Monday for the first time in months. Its foreign exchange reserves have been boosted by privatisation income and a flood of foreign investment in lev-denominated government securities offering high yields.
